title: AI security assessment or penetration test: what should you buy?
description: Compare an AI security assessment, penetration test and governance review. Define scope, evidence and acceptance criteria before buying security consulting.
audience: CTOs, product owners and security leads preparing an AI rollout
answer: Buy the assessment that answers your release decision. A penetration test looks for exploitable weaknesses in an agreed technical scope. An AI security assessment can also examine retrieval, model behaviour and agent permissions. A governance review examines responsibilities and evidence. These scopes overlap, but the labels alone do not tell you what will be tested.

sections.title: Start with a decision, not a scanner
paragraphs: Write down what you need to decide: whether an internal assistant can access customer files, whether an agent may update the CRM, or whether a supplier integration is ready for a pilot. Then name the systems, users and actions involved. A quote for an unspecified ‘AI audit’ leaves too much room for mismatched expectations.

Our suggested brief has five lines: business purpose, data involved, permitted actions, release deadline and accountable decision-maker. Attach an architecture sketch and identify the environment available for authorised testing. Keep production customer data out of initial enquiry forms.

sections.title: Compare the evidence each scope should produce
paragraphs: For a web or API penetration test, ask which authentication flows, roles, endpoints and tenant boundaries are included. For an AI assessment, add retrieval permissions, unsafe tool actions, misleading outputs and external content that can influence the model. For governance work, ask which decisions, records and control owners will be reviewed.

OWASP describes excessive agency as risk arising from excessive functionality, permissions or autonomy. NIST’s AI RMF offers a voluntary framework for managing AI risk. Neither reference turns a limited engagement into a complete compliance assessment. [1][2]

sections.title: Use a small acceptance matrix
paragraphs: The following is our illustrative procurement worksheet, not a claim about a client engagement. For each row, agree the setup, expected result, evidence and person accepting the outcome. Include both allowed and denied requests: a system that refuses everything is not a usable control.

sections.title: Make the report useful after the meeting
paragraphs: Request a finding register with affected component, prerequisites, observed behaviour, business consequence, suggested remediation and limitations. Ask for enough evidence to reproduce a finding safely, with secrets and personal data removed. Separate confirmed findings from hypotheses that need more access or time.

Agree whether remediation support and retesting are included. A successful retest concerns the tested fix in the tested version; it does not certify every path through a changing AI system. Record unresolved issues, compensating controls and who accepts residual risk before expanding access.

rows: Can one customer retrieve another customer’s information?
Allowed and denied retrieval cases, including source links and cached answers.
Can an assistant perform an unapproved write?
A controlled test showing the action is blocked at the tool or service boundary.
Can the team explain a failed control?
A reproducible finding, named owner and an agreed retest condition.
checklist: Name the applications, model configuration, integrations and test environment.
Set written authorisation, data-handling rules and stop conditions.
Specify test coverage, exclusions and the evidence format.
Agree how critical findings are escalated during the engagement.
Separate initial assessment, remediation and retest costs.
faq: Is an AI assessment a replacement for a penetration test?
Not automatically. An AI feature still depends on web, API and cloud controls. Agree coverage of both conventional attack paths and AI-specific behaviour, or commission complementary scopes.
Compare environments, identities, integrations, manual testing, deliverables and retest allowance. A lower price can reflect a narrower scope; ask what decision the work actually supports.

ctaText: Bring the product, its data flows and the decision blocking release. We can scope the assessment and the evidence your team needs.

title: MCP security: seven questions before connecting an AI agent
description: Review MCP server access, OAuth tokens, tool permissions and approvals before connecting AI agents to business systems. A practical buyer’s checklist.
audience: Teams connecting AI assistants to documents, CRM or developer tools
answer: Treat an MCP connection as a new route into your systems. Before enabling it, identify the server operator, the identity used for each action, the data it can access and how access can be revoked. Model Context Protocol standardises interactions; your deployment still needs its own security decisions and tests.

sections.title: Draw the connection before approving it
paragraphs: List the assistant, MCP client, server, downstream API and account used at each boundary. Mark where tokens, retrieved content and action logs travel. A connection described as ‘read-only’ in a demo can still use a service account with broader permissions underneath.

For a local server, review the executable, installation source, update path and access to local files or environment variables. For a remote server, review hosting, authentication, tenant isolation and the operator’s incident contact. These are different deployment questions; do not apply an HTTP OAuth checklist blindly to every local process.

sections.title: Check tokens and tool authority separately
paragraphs: The MCP specification’s HTTP authorisation guidance requires tokens intended for the receiving server and prohibits passing the client’s token straight through to another API. Confirm the protocol version your implementation follows. [1]

Authentication does not answer whether a particular action is appropriate. OWASP’s excessive-agency guidance supports limiting available functions and privileges and independently approving high-impact actions. [2] Our practical recommendation is to request the smallest tool set that completes the actual workflow, then test denied actions as well as successful ones.

sections.title: Use these seven questions in the supplier meeting
paragraphs: Ask for evidence from your proposed configuration, not a generic security slide. Record an owner and follow-up date for each unanswered question. A missing answer is a reason to narrow the pilot until the uncertainty is resolved; it is not, by itself, proof that a supplier has been compromised.

sections.title: Run a bounded pilot before expanding access
paragraphs: Our illustrative pilot uses a separate test workspace, synthetic documents and one harmless write operation. Establish a successful authorised request, then check an unauthorised account, a revoked permission and an attempt to reach a resource outside scope. Keep testing within written permission and agreed limits.

Record the requested action, effective identity, approval result and downstream outcome without copying secrets into logs. Practise disabling the connection and confirm that new requests are denied. Cached data and already-issued downstream sessions may need separate cleanup. Define what must be retested when tools, server versions or access scopes change.

tableTitle: A connection register you can use
rows: Connection and owner
Client, server operator, deployment type and responsible business owner.
Authority
Allowed tools, effective identities, permitted resources and approval boundary.
Recovery
Revocation procedure, retained data, incident contact and next review trigger.
checklist: Who operates and updates this MCP server?
Which identity reaches the downstream system?
Which records can it read, change, delete or export?
How are token audience, storage and expiry handled?
Where are consequential actions approved outside model judgement?
What evidence is logged, and who can inspect it?
How do we revoke access and verify that revocation worked?
faq: Does using MCP make an agent secure?
No. A protocol does not validate your chosen permissions, server implementation or business workflow. Review the actual deployment and the systems it can reach.
Is a private MCP server always safer?
Not necessarily. Hosting location is one factor. A private server with excessive permissions, poor updates or weak logging can still create significant exposure.

title: AI-generated code: a security review before you ship
description: A practical DevSecOps checklist for AI-generated code: access controls, dependencies, CI/CD permissions, secrets and evidence for a safer release.
audience: Engineering leads shipping AI-assisted code or no-code prototypes
answer: Review AI-generated code as production code: establish ownership, test access boundaries, inspect dependencies and control the release pipeline. A working demo and a clean scanner report are useful inputs, but neither shows that the application enforces the business rules your customers depend on.

sections.title: Start with the changes that carry authority
paragraphs: Prioritise authentication, authorisation, payments, uploads, data exports and administrative actions. Ask a reviewer to explain what each sensitive change does and why the caller is allowed to do it. If nobody can explain the control, keep that change out of production until the team can review it properly.

Our suggested review record names the commit, affected feature, data touched, reviewer and acceptance test. Identify generated migrations and infrastructure changes as well as application code. A small interface change can conceal a much larger change to database access or deployment privileges.

sections.title: Test the business boundary, not just the happy path
paragraphs: Create paired tests: an authorised user can perform the operation, while an unauthorised user cannot. Include another tenant, an expired session and a request that bypasses the interface. For retrieval features, test whether the service excludes documents the current user cannot access before they enter the model context.

Microsoft’s Azure AI Search documentation distinguishes service-level roles from document-level access controls. That distinction matters when reviewing a RAG feature: permission to query a service is not automatically permission to read every document. [1] The exact configuration and available features depend on your chosen implementation.

sections.title: Protect the route from pull request to deployment
paragraphs: GitHub’s secure-use guidance recommends minimal workflow token permissions and warns about untrusted input and code in privileged workflows. It also documents OIDC for cloud authentication where supported. [2] Review both the pipeline configuration and the cloud trust policy; adopting a mechanism does not validate its settings.

For your release checklist, require an accountable owner for dependency updates, secret findings and build failures. Pin dependencies or actions according to the project’s update policy, verify where packages come from and review newly added install scripts. Avoid letting a generated workflow grant broad permissions merely to make a failing build pass.

sections.title: Leave a release record the next engineer can use
paragraphs: Our proposed handover contains the reviewed commit, test results, dependency changes, known limitations and rollback procedure. Record why an exception was accepted and when it expires. A scanner finding needs a disposition; silently ignoring it is not the same as assessing it.

After deployment, check the intended behaviour and the failure paths that matter to customers. Confirm who handles alerts and whether the previous version can be restored without losing required data. Use new privileged integrations, changed data flows and major dependency updates as triggers for another review.

tableTitle: Three checks that deserve release evidence
rows: User and tenant access
Paired allowed/denied API tests, including direct requests.
Build identity
Workflow permissions and cloud trust conditions reviewed together.
Change recovery
An agreed rollback procedure and ownership of unresolved findings.
checklist: A named engineer can explain sensitive code and infrastructure changes.
Authentication and authorisation are checked on the server.
Dependencies, install scripts and secret findings have been reviewed.
Untrusted pull requests cannot inherit deployment authority.
Tests cover denied actions, not only successful demonstrations.
The release has an owner, known limitations and a recovery plan.
faq: Can a scanner replace a manual review?

A scanner can identify classes of problems within its coverage. It cannot, by itself, establish whether your application implements the intended business permissions or whether an exception is acceptable.
Should we ban AI coding tools?
A tool ban is a policy choice, not a substitute for delivery controls. Define approved tools and data use, then require accountable review and evidence for code regardless of how it was produced.
ctaTitle: Your prototype works. Is the delivery path ready?
ctaText: We can review the agreed route from repository to release and help your team make security checks repeatable.

title: What does secure AI automation cost? Build a useful ROI case
description: Calculate AI automation value using real task volumes, review time and operating costs. Includes a worked example and a buyer’s scope checklist.
audience: Operations leaders and founders evaluating an automation budget
answer: Estimate value per completed task, including human review and failures. Compare that value with implementation, integration, security and ongoing operating costs. Time released is capacity, not automatically cash saved. The best first project is one with a measurable bottleneck, usable data and a clear owner for exceptions.

sections.title: Measure the existing workflow first
paragraphs: Choose one task, such as preparing an internal support response or classifying an incoming request. Record monthly volume, handling time, error rate and rework. Use observed samples across normal and difficult cases rather than the fastest demonstration. Separate waiting time from hands-on work so you do not count the same benefit twice.

Our planning worksheet records the baseline, proposed workflow, acceptance criteria and person who can redeploy any released capacity. If the organisation cannot use the time saved, the financial case should not treat it as an immediate reduction in payroll.

sections.title: Include the costs that arrive after the demo
paragraphs: Budget for integration, data preparation, identity and access, testing, training and handover. For ongoing operation, include model and cloud charges, human review, support, monitoring and changes to connected systems. Ask what happens to the quote if a supplier API changes or a new approval step becomes necessary.

Microsoft’s cost-optimisation guidance recommends a maintained cost model aligned with business value. NIST’s Manage guidance calls for weighing AI benefits against negative risks. [1][2] Our commercial application of those ideas is to make security and exception handling explicit cost items before comparing proposals.

sections.title: Worked example: capacity is not the same as savings
paragraphs: This is a fictional planning example, not a client result or a SundAI price. Assume 1,200 tasks a month, six minutes of manual work per task and two minutes after automation, including review. That releases 4,800 minutes, or 80 hours. At an illustrative loaded labour value of €35 per hour, capacity value is €2,800 per month.

If incremental operating costs are €900 per month and implementation costs €12,000, the simple net capacity-value estimate is €1,900 per month. Dividing €12,000 by €1,900 gives about 6.3 months. This is a capacity-value payback illustration, not a cash-payback forecast. It excludes financing, tax and ramp-up, and assumes every released hour is productively used.

If review takes four minutes instead, only 40 hours are released. Their illustrative value is €1,400; after €900 operating cost, the difference is €500 and the same calculation becomes 24 months. Small changes in real review effort can matter more than a cheap model subscription.

sections.title: Agree a pilot decision before buying a rollout
paragraphs: Set a minimum usable output rate, maximum review effort and acceptable exception path for your actual workflow. Assign somebody to inspect failures and record costs during the pilot. Avoid expanding permissions just to reach a speed target; that changes the risk as well as the economics.

At the decision meeting, choose to proceed, narrow the scope or stop. A useful pilot can show that ordinary rules-based automation is sufficient, that data needs preparation, or that human handling remains preferable. Capture the reasoning so the next project starts with evidence instead of another optimistic demo.

checklist: Task volume and measured handling time, including difficult cases.
Systems and data the workflow needs to access.

Implementation budget and ongoing cost assumptions.
How released capacity will be used and how success will be measured.
faq: Can you quote an automation project from the task name alone?
A useful quote needs the systems, data, permissions, integrations and acceptance criteria. Two workflows with the same name can require very different implementation and assurance work.
What does the €490 AI Decision Review cover?
One AI decision, a 45-minute discussion and a 3–5-page memo. Scope, timing and applicable VAT are confirmed before acceptance. It is separate from implementation or a technical security assessment.
